# Psalm 21: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I found and what's missing.** I found good verse-by-verse material from Guzik, Spurgeon, Matthew Henry, Calvin, Barnes, the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott, Gill, the Cambridge Bible, Clarke, Coffman and Augustine. I found nothing from Wesley's own notes, the Lutheran sites, the Orthodox sites, the NET Bible's translator notes, Bible Odyssey, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace writers, so those are left out. Two of the pages I read (the full Pulpit Commentary page and Augustine's full exposition) came without markers that let me cite exact sentences, so for those points I just give the URL.

---

## Overview

- Psalm 21 follows on from Psalm 20. The victory prayed for there has now happened, and David thanks God for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Some link the psalm to the aftermath of a decisive battle, possibly against the Ammonites (2 Samuel 10–12). https://biblehub.com/psalms/21.htm 
- **Shape of the psalm:** praise for God's strength in v. 1 is answered by praise for God's strength in v. 13. https://biblehub.com/psalms/21.htm 
- **David or Christ?** Matthew Henry reads it as David first, with an eye to Christ, whose victories over evil David's victories only foreshadowed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_021.cfm 
- **Jewish reading:** Guzik says early Jewish interpreters took the psalm as being about the Messiah, and that this reading was dropped in the Middle Ages partly to counter Christian use of it. He holds that both readings apply. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/  Clarke notes that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) renders "the king" as "the King Messiah." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-1.html 

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- The future tense ("shall joy") expresses continuing joy: the king rejoices and will keep rejoicing. The salvation hoped for in Psalm 20 has now been experienced. (Pulpit) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-1.htm 
- Barnes: "strength" means the success came from God alone, not from the king's skill or courage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-1.htm 
- Calvin: David could have thanked God privately, but he wanted to show that God's favour to him benefited all the faithful. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-1.html 
- Spurgeon applies the verse to the risen Christ, who as a man drew his strength from God in prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-1.htm 
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon saying the early Methodists' joyful shouting was more excusable than our lukewarm worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 

**v. 2**
- Guzik: God answered both the desire of David's heart and his spoken prayers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Matthew Henry: no prayer is accepted unless it is truly the heart's desire. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-1.html 
- Pulpit: the pause at "Selah" may have been for presenting a thank-offering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- Guzik's summary lists many hindrances to answered prayer, such as unbelief, unconfessed sin and selfish motives. He adds that avoiding them does not earn God's answer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Augustine (Catholic reading) applies the verse to Christ: his desire to eat the Passover and to lay down his life and take it up again. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm 

**v. 3**
- "Welcomed/meet him" (KJV "preventest") means God goes ahead of us. Guzik says God brought the blessings to David, rather than David chasing them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/  Pulpit: God gives blessings before he is asked, and more than is asked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- **The crown:** Pulpit notes that David did take the Ammonite king's gold crown (2 Samuel 12:30), but thinks the verse means God granting him rule, tied to the promises to David in 2 Samuel 7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm Guzik: David waited for God to put the crown on him rather than seizing it from Saul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Augustine reads the "precious stones" in his Latin text as Christ's disciples gathered round him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm 

**v. 4: a verse where readings really differ**
- **The king's line lives on (Pulpit, Barnes):** this cannot mean ordinary human life, since David did not live forever. Pulpit says it means his line continuing, as promised through Nathan, with the full meaning found only in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm  Barnes: God gave more than David asked, the promise that he would live on in his descendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-21.html 
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God gave a man near death not only his life but a kingdom passed down to his descendants forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/21.htm 
- **Kidner, quoted by Guzik:** an Old Testament reader might have taken "forever" as exaggeration or as the endless dynasty, but in Christ the words are true without exaggeration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- **Christ's resurrection (Spurgeon's collected notes, and Augustine):** Christ asked to be raised ("Father, glorify thy Son") and was given it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps021.cfm  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm
- **Messiah only (Coffman):** the king here cannot be any earthly ruler; he is the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-1.html 

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: this salvation is partly earthly (rescue from enemies) and partly spiritual, through David's link to the coming Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- Guzik: David saw his glory as coming from God, not from himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Augustine: the glory of the resurrection, with more added when Christ is seated at the Father's right hand. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: literally "you set him to be blessings forever," that is, a lasting source of blessing to others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm 
- Guzik: God's presence thrilled David more than the crown did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Guzik also says Jesus, though a man of sorrows, knew what it was to be glad. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/  Spurgeon similarly calls Jesus' joy full, divine in source and eternal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps021.cfm 
- Barnes: "forever" points to the eternal blessings that come through the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-21.html 

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: trust is both the reason for God's favour and the result of it. But the confidence of "not be shaken" did not always hold for David; see Psalm 30:6–7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- Matthew Henry: because the king trusts God, his people are encouraged. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_021.cfm 
- Augustine: the King is humble, not proud, and hopes in the Lord. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm 

**v. 8: who is being addressed?**
- The BSB takes "You" to be God. Ellicott, though, says the psalm now turns to speak to the king. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-21.html  Constable agrees: the change of person shows David's subjects now addressing him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-9.html 
- Pulpit: "find out" means reach and punish. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-21.html 
- Guzik: God was not finished dealing with his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Augustine: Christ's power, which his enemies did not recognise in his humble state, will find them at the judgment. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm

**v. 9: literal, figurative or final judgment?**
- **The wording:** "time of Your anger" is literally "time of your face," meaning your appearing. (Ellicott) https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-21.html  Ellicott also suggests a slight change to the Hebrew, "put them into a fiery oven," with the picture taken from a smelter's furnace. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-21.html 
- **Figurative, about David's wars (Pulpit):** "fiery oven" is probably a metaphor, though it points to the severe treatment David gave captured enemies (2 Samuel 12:31). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-9.htm  The Cambridge Bible also sees a possible reference to the Ammonites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-9.htm 
- **Final judgment:** Coffman places it at Christ's second coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-9.html  Bible Hub's own study notes call it a "sure, literal, fiery judgment." https://biblehub.com/psalms/21-9.htm 
- **Gill (Baptist):** being "swallowed up" does not mean the wicked cease to exist; they suffer God's wrath forever. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/psalms/21-9.html 
- **Calvin:** this is aimed at those who violently despise God and rise up against his Son, not at every enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-9.html 
- **Inner torment (Matthew Henry):** the wicked become their own fiery oven through a guilty conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/21-9.html  Augustine reads it the same way: first their own conscience burns them, then eternal fire. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: now is the time of grace, and there will be a set time for wrath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Geneva Bible note: this teaches us to bear trouble patiently until God destroys the enemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-9.htm 

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: "fruit" means offspring. Compare Joab cutting off every male in Edom (1 Kings 11:16). The second line simply repeats the first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- Delitzsch (on Bible Hub): this was the fate of the Amalekites, here foretold for the king's enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-9.htm 
- Guzik: David is confident God will judge even the descendants of those who fight him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Augustine takes "seed" as their works, or the people they led astray. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: they bring destruction on themselves. Their intention is enough, even if they achieve nothing, and their plans fail because God opposes them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- Guzik: deliberate rebellion is worse than sins of ignorance, and it is a comfort that their plots cannot succeed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-21/ 
- Augustine applies it to Caiaphas's plan that "one die for all" (John 11:50). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: literally "make them turn the neck," meaning put them to flight. The KJV adds the words "when" and "thine arrows" to fill out what the psalmist leaves unsaid. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: "Be exalted" means be lifted up, both in yourself and in your people's praise. The psalm ends as it began, praising God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/21.htm
- Barnes's doxology note (as quoted on Bible Hub) says this may close both Psalms 20 and 21, and honours God's grace in every age, including under Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/21-1.htm 
- Augustine: God's strength, which his enemies took for weakness, is now exalted. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801021.htm

## Where the traditions differ

I found no sharp split along denominational lines on this psalm. The real differences cut across traditions:

1. **v. 4:** does "life forever" mean David's dynasty (Pulpit, Barnes, Calvin), Christ's resurrection (Spurgeon's notes, Augustine), or only the Messiah (Coffman)?
2. **v. 8:** is God or the king being addressed?
3. **v. 9:** is the fire David's warfare, the final judgment, or a guilty conscience?

Calvin (Reformed), Gill and Spurgeon (Baptist), Clarke (Methodist) and Guzik (Calvary Chapel, listed under enduringword.com) all read the psalm as pointing to Christ in some way.
